CRUD using ADO.NET without Entity Framework

Follow one SQL parameter from the incoming request into the database command.

Open interactive lesson and complete code

What you are building

A student register that runs SQL commands

Build an API that sends parameterised SQL commands through ADO.NET. You write the SQL used to add, find, edit and remove rows.

Student data is stored in SQL Server. Run the supplied setup script first.

Check the result

Create the table, send a student request and check the row in SQL Server.

ADO.NET is the more hands-on route. You write SQL, add typed parameters, open a connection and read results yourself.

How to test this example in Visual Studio

Download the project below, extract it into its own folder, then open StudyLab.csproj. Wait for NuGet restore. Choose Build → Build Solution. For console projects choose Start Without Debugging. For API projects use View → Terminal, make sure the terminal is in the folder containing StudyLab.csproj, then run the command shown in the lesson. Do not paste all files into Program.cs: use the exact file names displayed below.

Install and create the right project

  • Install Visual Studio with ASP.NET and web development and a .NET 10-compatible SDK. For WPF also install .NET desktop development. Check Tools → Get Tools and Features if templates are missing.
  • Create ASP.NET Core Empty for the Minimal API, or ASP.NET Core Web API with Use controllers for a controller project. Select .NET 10. Alternatively open the supplied .csproj to get exactly the lesson files.
  • Use a separate folder for every example. Delete the generated weather sample if it conflicts with the supplied files. Restore NuGet packages before building.
  • In View → Terminal, cd into the folder containing StudyLab.csproj. For local API testing run dotnet run --urls http://localhost:5100. Open requests.http and use Send Request above each request. Use the actual port from the console if you launch with a different profile.

Your first request

GET http://localhost:5100/api/students

Initially expect 200 OK with []. A browser address bar can send GET, but cannot conveniently send all CRUD methods. Use the .http editor, Postman, curl.exe or a Swagger UI. The JSON object is a data packet, not an HTML page.

Prepare the database

Open setup.sql in SSMS connected to your local SQL Server. Run it once to create StudyLabAdo and Students. GO is an SSMS batch separator, not a command to send through SqlCommand. The schema already exists in this example, so EF migrations are not used. Microsoft.Data.SqlClient supplies SqlConnection, SqlCommand and SqlDataReader.

Understand the methods

  • SqlConnection describes a connection; OpenAsync actually opens it. await using disposes it after the operation. Connection pooling can reuse physical connections.
  • SqlCommand holds the SQL and parameters. Parameters carry values separately from SQL text. Never concatenate names or search input into a SQL statement.
  • ExecuteReaderAsync returns rows. ReadAsync moves to the next row; GetInt32 and GetString read typed columns in SELECT order.
  • ExecuteScalarAsync returns one value, here the inserted identity from OUTPUT INSERTED.Id. ExecuteNonQueryAsync returns affected-row information for updates/deletes.
  • The full controller implements all five resource routes with cancellation and validation. This is an alternative to EF, not an extra layer required by EF.

Parameters and expected results

cmd.Parameters.Add("@name", SqlDbType.NVarChar, 80).Value = input.Name.Trim();
cmd.Parameters.Add("@age", SqlDbType.Int).Value = input.Age;

A name containing an apostrophe should still save as text. The CRUD response sequence is the same as the EF controller. If UPDATE affects zero rows, return 404 instead of pretending a change happened.

Try it yourself

Fix: "WHERE Name = '" + input + "'".

Worked answer

Use WHERE Name=@name and add an NVarChar parameter. Parameters are for values; validate/allowlist any selectable column names separately.

Why dispose a reader before reusing the connection for another command?

Worked answer

An open reader can hold the connection busy. Finish reading and dispose it; do not rely on a reader disappearing by itself.

Predict and practise

Should user text be joined into an SQL command string?

Check your prediction

No. Pass values as typed SQL parameters.

Make one change

Trace the Name parameter from input through the INSERT command.

Worked guidance

Find the parameter placeholder and the matching Parameters.Add call.

Try independently

Add and edit a student whose name contains an apostrophe. Check the stored name.
